chapter_theme: The queen, taken by the night song of the elephant-keeper, confesses to her friend Gunavati, who first pleads restraint and recoils from the keeper's ugliness, then goes to him as go-between; he refuses from fear of the king and is brought round, and the queen turns cold to the king and slips away from his bed.

cast.role: the king's chief queen, who falls in love with the elephant-keeper
the hunchbacked elephant-keeper who sings by night

96.reading: The poet remarks that a desiring mind is less steady than lightning, that the purity of good company and counsel fall away, and that the woman fears no later blame and holds her own worth cheap.
96.nuance: The last line is hard to parse; it seems to close the poet's comment on the queen's fall by saying she became one who set these warnings aside, but the grammar could also give it as the words of someone else.

claims.claim: a mind that wants something is less steady than lightning, and company and counsel cannot hold it

97.reading: The night over, the queen sits alone, holding the sweet singer in her heart; her friend comes close and, finding her lost in thought as if her husband were away, asks her to say what she is thinking.
97.event: The queen sits through the dawn thinking of the singer; her friend finds her so and asks what troubles her.

98.reading: The queen tells her friend that her mind, like a dark rutting elephant that lived on the king's dignity, has been seized by the goad of a night singer's tune and made to waver in distress.
98.nuance: The image makes the queen's mind a elephant fed on the king's dignity and mastered by a goad that is his song, so her fall is told as capture rather than choice.
98.event: The queen confesses to her friend that a man's night singing has overturned her mind.

99.reading: Gunavati, making as if she did not know what is in the queen's heart, answers back and tells her that her greatness is real, and that she should not grieve over a fault seen in a dream.
99.nuance: The friend's feigned ignorance (அறிந்தனல்லளேபோல்) is the poet's report of her pretence, so her answer here is a deflection, not yet an argument.
99.event: Gunavati answers the queen's confession by treating her trouble as a dream-fault and asking her not to grieve.

100.reading: The queen thinks her friend has not understood her sickness and says so openly; Gunavati rebukes her for putting into words what is not in her real mind and gently stops her ears.
100.nuance: The friend's first response is refusal, set against her later service as go-between from verse 110.
100.event: The queen declares her desire plainly; Gunavati covers her ears and rebukes her for saying it.

101.reading: The queen says that if they refuse to hear the song of the man with the nectar mouth, her life will end that very day, and asks the friend to give an answer.
101.event: The queen tells her friend that she will die if she is denied the singer.

102.reading: The queen says that the man who tied her life to his sweet music has no equal, tells her friend to decide quickly, and warns that delay would hurt her and bring blame; the friend, who had not thought with her, now thinks the matter through.
102.event: The queen urges her friend to decide quickly; the friend begins to weigh it.

103.reading: At night the friend goes in the dark to find who the man with the flowing voice is, finds him with a ghoul-like form, and returns glad that the queen's passion will end.
103.nuance: The friend's relief rests on the idea that his ugliness will cool the queen's desire; the next verses show the idea carried to the queen as a remedy, and it fails.
103.event: Gunavati goes by night, finds the singer, sees his frightful form and goes back relieved.

104.reading: The friend tells the queen that the singer of the song that tormented her is the elephant-keeper Ashtavakran, that she shut her eyes at the sight of his body and came away, and asks not to be blamed since she could not give him the queen's message.
104.event: Gunavati reports to the queen that the singer is the elephant-keeper Ashtavakran and that she turned back in revulsion.

105.reading: The friend describes him: a body tied with sinews, a sunk neck, withered fingers, a small angry face like a monkey's, a hunched back, caved-in eyes and a few crooked teeth.
105.nuance: The list is the friend's argument by loathing; it is not the poet's own account of him.
105.event: Gunavati lists his deformities to the queen.

106.reading: The friend adds that his body is foul with sores, his eyes are not what they should be and his caste is unfit, and she asks the queen to let her sinking heart go and to shut up her self-restraint.
106.nuance: The queen's answer in verses 107 and 108 sets the argument aside rather than answering it on its own terms, so the claims are the friend's.
106.event: Gunavati pleads with the queen to give up the keeper and keep her self-restraint.

claims.claim: a man of low birth and a sore-ridden body is not a fit object of a queen's desire
a woman should confine her heart's restraint and let her desire go

107.reading: The queen answers that because of these very things her desire for him grew, and she lists wealth, valour, splendour, beauty, learning and family as gains made in the past, together with the hearts of the good.
107.nuance: The syntax of the whole verse turns on a phrase of the fruit that stands (நின்று செய் பயன்) that the verse leaves bare; I read it as a past-deed claim spoken to turn the friend's reasons about birth and body.
107.event: The queen answers her friend by listing the goods that are the fruit of earlier deeds.

claims.claim: wealth, power, beauty, learning and birth are the fruit of what one stood and did before

108.reading: The queen says that once the thing has come about it is no business to search out its cause, that the god of love bestows grace on anyone, and that the friend should go quickly and finish the matter.
108.event: The queen tells her friend that her love needs no justification and sends her to fetch the keeper.

claims.claim: once an effect has come about, hunting for its cause is not a task; the god of love gives his grace to whom he will

109.reading: The friend, shaken, says that the queen is as a Lakshmi, that the man has been taken into her gracious mind, and that the life-taking disease will become a hound of fault; she cries out at how the flower-arrowed god had joined this and stands trembling.
109.nuance: The middle two lines are hard; the word for a dog (ஞமலி) is read as a figure for the shame the disease will bring.
109.event: Gunavati, trembling, wonders at how the god of love has brought the queen to this.

110.reading: After thinking it through, the friend reasons that she is a great woman given by the creator and turns away to go, resolved.
110.nuance: The first three lines name men and the learned and renouncing; the sense of how they bear on her reasoning is unclear, and only the friend's decision to go is plain.
110.event: Gunavati weighs the matter and decides to go to the keeper.

111.reading: She goes to a corner hall where he lies asleep, his body stinking, wrapped in filthy cloth and covered with dust, and in a troubled mind tells him the king's queen's desire.
111.event: Gunavati finds the keeper asleep in a filthy hall and tells him of the queen's desire.

112.reading: Hearing it, he is filled with fear, says ruin has come upon him and that the king will kill him, rebukes her for speaking unworthily and bids her go; she shows him what she can and breaks down his resolve.
112.event: Ashtavakran, frightened, refuses and tells her to go; she overcomes his fear.

claims.claim: a man who touches the king's queen will be put to death by the king

113.reading: He says that he has had the fruit of merit, that a man with a sore body and dust-rolling hands who wins the heart of the king's queen has gained more than any famed ascetic, and that this is his boon.
113.nuance: The boast puts a woman's sin into the language of karmic reward; it is the keeper's voice, and the poem does not endorse it.
113.event: Ashtavakran, won over, calls the queen's love the best fruit of his past merit.

claims.claim: winning the queen's heart is the fruit of earlier merit, greater than the fruit of renowned austerity

114.reading: After telling him the queen's time and sign she goes back; the queen, burning like evening in the fire of desire, asks her to say how her errand went.
114.event: Gunavati returns from the keeper and the queen asks for her news.

115.reading: The friend says all has gone well, and tells how she met the keeper, how he flared up in anger, how she brought him round, and the sign for the meeting; the queen is delighted.
115.event: Gunavati reports the keeper's anger, his yielding and the signal for the tryst.

116.reading: The queen goes to join the man the friend has brought, her words sweet with desire, and turns her ill-will on the king and no longer treats him with her old sweetness, which the king notices and wonders at.
116.nuance: The order of the lines suggests the meeting and the king's puzzlement as one passage, but the grammar of the first two lines is not clear.
116.event: The queen meets the keeper through her friend, while the king notices that she has turned cold to him.

117.reading: Leaving the court, the king lies on his bed in a rage that he does not voice, as if asleep; the queen, taking his sleep for real, leaves with her friend for the tryst place.
117.event: The king lies feigning sleep on his bed, and the queen goes off with Gunavati to the meeting place.

links.note: In 103 the friend is glad that the keeper's form will end the queen's passion; in 111 the same friend carries the queen's desire to that body.
links.teaches: The sight meant to cure the queen's desire turns into the errand that fulfils it, so loathing proves no barrier once the friend takes the queen's side.

links.note: The keeper first refuses from fear of the king, and the friend's persuasion turns him to count the queen's love a prize.
links.teaches: His boast of reward is bought by overcoming the very fear he voiced, which shows how little weighing of cost enters the match.

links.note: In 97 the queen is alone in thought while the king is by; in 117 she leaves the sleeping king for the keeper.
links.teaches: The inward desire of the first night becomes the act of the night the king watches, so the poem takes her from thought to deed.

links.note: In 106 the friend urges the queen to shut up her restraint and drop the keeper; in 110 she resolves to go to him.
links.teaches: The friend's refusal gives way within a few verses, so the poem shows restraint offered by an attendant as only as strong as her pity.

links.note: The friend asks the queen to confine her restraint; the couplet says desire breaks that bolted door.
links.teaches: The couplet's door of restraint is shown here as one a friend urges the queen to keep shut and which the queen has already broken.

gains.a: the plea to imprison restraint is shown as too late, since the couplet says desire already breaks the door it names
gains.b: the couplet, spoken in a woman's voice, gets a case where another woman tells a queen to hold the door and cannot

links.note: The friend answers desire by loathing the body's foulness, as the quatrain does with every body.
links.teaches: The remedy of disgust works in the quatrain as meditation and fails in the story, where one repellent body cannot cool a mind already taken.

gains.a: her appeal to the keeper's sores and deformity is shown as a kind of the meditation, but aimed at one man, so it lacks the quatrain's reach
gains.b: the quatrain's instruction to see the body as a bag turned inside out is tried on a real person and is found weaker than the desire it was meant to quiet

links.note: The quatrain weighs great fear against small pleasure and counsels against another's wife; the keeper, who has just said the king will kill him, then calls the queen's love his best reward.
links.teaches: The quatrain's reckoning of fear against pleasure is tested on a man who does the sum and then goes ahead.

gains.a: the keeper's boast is set against the king's sword he named in 112, so his reward reads as a risk he has chosen to ignore
gains.b: the quatrain's prudence gets a speaker who has done the sum and gone past it, which the plain rule does not allow for

links.note: The queen leaves the king for the keeper, as the verse says men leave the ripe jackfruit for the thorny date.
links.teaches: The poem uses the Tirumanthiram's choice of poor fruit over rich fruit for a woman, and for a far more extreme pair.

gains.a: her turning from the king is named as a choice of the worse fruit, which the epic's narration leaves to the reader
gains.b: the image of the jackfruit and the date, spoken of men, is shown to hold for a woman and for the sharpest contrast of rank and body

links.note: The poet says a desiring mind outruns counsel; the verse says even learned men and yogis cannot turn a mind once bewildered.
links.teaches: The queen's fall is made one case of a general weakness that knowledge and attainment do not guard against.

gains.a: the queen's loss of restraint is set beside the learned and the yogis, which makes her case a human one and not only a woman's
gains.b: the verse's claim that attainment gives no protection gets a case where even a queen with every comfort is undone by one night's song

source_issues: Verse 99 line 4 and 107 line 4 are hard to construe and the readings are cautious.
